Offason, Mercia, United Kingdom, 6 years ago

Realist - With all respect to yourself, I would like to add a little to your post addressed to our resident dimwit, Kevin on the subject of chance in relation to chemical reactions. Put simply, atoms consist of a heavy nucleus containing protons and neutrons. We can think of this as being surrounded by a number of electrons (the same number as that of the protons). These electrons are organised in shells, similar to the orbits of planets around our sun. Many atoms have an outer shell that is lacking one electron needed for orbital stability. If it meets another atom with one more electron than is needed for a stable shell, the two "react" by sharing their electrons, thus forming a compound with a lower-energy electron cloud. Atoms will always react spontaneously and need no external direction. I am sure you know this but it is for the benefit of ordinary readers who have not studied physical chemistry.

aquarianprime - I am sorry but you are wrong. When abiogenesis initiated on this planet, the first step was the evolution of self-replicating molecules. These formed because of the natural affinity of atoms to each other. About seven years ago, UCL reported in the scientific press that they had achieved this. About the same time, another lab reported the spontaneous formation of fatty membranes in aqueous clay suspensions. So, we have the two components of a cellular nucleus - - the molecule (RNA or DNA) and a protective membrane. Millions of years later, the retro viruses evolved. These behave as a big molecule, spontaneously initiating their own duplication and - - catalyse the reaction so that it proceeds vastly more rapidly. These retroviruses are with us still but now hijack cells, which evolved about a billion years later.
